codex.worst_flaw: The safety gate is insufficient for launch because it audits only credited jobs and can miss skipped or degraded safety checks on fallback and other uncredited jobs.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning and audit design is underspecified: crews are randomised only 'where scheduling permits', with no sample-size or power check, no handling of spillover between crews or route connectivity mix, no predefined cost or harm thresholds, and no replayable event and policy versioning or independent shadow validation of credit before payout.

holistic.reason: Unusually well-designed for a unionised workforce, with union co-design, a fallback that doesn't penalise failure, a quality gate against gaming, and a comparison group, but a pooled 55% team-break target is a modest, easily-missed motivator, and the gains depend on fixing app friction rather than on the reward, so noticing is mixed and persistence rests mostly on those fixes.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch blocker: The payout rule uses started jobs as its denominator but leaves credit undefined when a technician files a valid hazard checklist and stops the job before work begins.

claude.worst_flaw: The group reward pays on raw pooled completion against a fixed 55% target, with no adjustment for crews' job mix, fallback rates or connectivity. The weekly progress feed is also capped at three jobs, so it gives almost no signal on most jobs and does not handle uneven workloads.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about union buy-in, denominator integrity, hazard-reporting protections, and randomised follow-up, but the reward of 30 minutes of paid time is modest, the checklist behaviour hinges on removing app friction that is not yet diagnosed, and gains driven by an extrinsic reward typically fade once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The 20-check weekly audit is too small to catch rushed or box-ticked checks across a 300-person workforce, and nothing checks the digital record against what actually happens on site (no field observation), so a high completion rate could hide checks that were never really done. The 15-point depot target also has no adjustment for small depots or job mix, and the event-replay and shadow-validation plan for appeals is thin.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the audit can independently verify that technicians perform the required safety checks, because job and hold records can miss checklists submitted without those checks.

holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous on diagnosis, safety-quality gates, union-aligned privacy and a fair crew-wide reward with a comparator, but the 30-minute paid-time reward is modest and collective, the credit rules are complex for technicians to grasp, and gains likely rest on app fixes more than incentives, so post-programme persistence is uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success by comparing the pilot with its own baseline, with no comparison group. It therefore cannot separate the reward's effect from routing fixes, seasonal workload or regression, and the same eight-working-hour deadline applies to every PR regardless of size or complexity.

codex.worst_flaw: The sequential pilot cannot tell whether the reward improved response times because changes in PR mix, workload, or familiarity with the new workflow could also explain the lift.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about fairness, auditing, privacy and a go/no-go gate, but it is heavy to run and the reward is a weak team-wide hour off, and the diagnosis is unverified, so sceptical engineers may barely notice it and gains probably fade once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The rollout rule can be triggered by changes in PR complexity or reviewer workload across periods because the evaluation accounts for neither.

claude.worst_flaw: The before/after baseline with no concurrent comparison group cannot separate the reward's effect from the routing and feedback support or from seasonal change in PR volume, and the design itself treats the result only as feasibility evidence.

holistic.reason: It is carefully built, with a diagnosis step, fair credit rules, private individual progress, quality sampling and a pilot-then-withdraw design. But it is heavy to run for 25 engineers, a one-hour reward is a weak lever against sceptics, and the 8-hour clock may not stick once support and the reward end.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success by comparing the pilot with the team's own baseline and has no comparison group, so seasonality, case mix and novelty effects could produce the 15-point gain that decides the rollout.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside routing fixes and private feedback, so it cannot establish whether paid time off adds value beyond those workflow improvements.

holistic.reason: It is a carefully designed, privacy-protective, team-level scheme with diagnosis, audits and a skeptic test that suit sceptical engineers, but a one-hour reward is a weak motivator, the metric is easy to game despite the audit, and the behaviour may fade once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a concurrent plain-feedback comparison, the pilot cannot tell whether the ward meal improves verified logging beyond feedback, kiosk fixes, and growing familiarity with the workflow.

claude.worst_flaw: The design rewards logging rates on wards whose clinical value to nurses is never shown, then judges success by each ward's own before-and-after change with no concurrent comparison or plain-feedback arm, so it cannot separate the incentive's effect from kiosk fixes, time trends or observer (Hawthorne) effects.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with strong safeguards (observer matching, pause rules, no discipline use), but heavy matching/audit overhead and a modest team meal reward make it feel burdensome and low-salience to nurses, and the effect likely fades once the reward and observation windows end.

codex.worst_flaw: The before-and-after pilot cannot isolate whether the catered break improves verified logging beyond private feedback and workflow fixes.

claude.worst_flaw: Rewarding verified kiosk logging still has no proven link to better hand hygiene or patient outcomes, and the evaluation is only a baseline-versus-reward comparison with no concurrent control ward, so it cannot separate the reward's effect from observer presence, seasonality or plain workflow support.

holistic.reason: Carefully designed with strong safeguards (safety pauses, no disciplinary reuse, separation of logging credit from clinical compliance), but it is complex and admin-heavy, the kiosk's purpose is vague to nurses, the reward is a modest ward-level catered break, and logging is a side task that likely fades once rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: The decision to expand rests on a pre/post comparison across three pooled wards with no concurrent control ward, so seasonal effects and observer-driven behaviour change (Hawthorne effects) cannot be separated from the effect of the reward. The design also never questions whether logging every hand-hygiene moment is worth the documentation burden it puts on nurses.

codex.worst_flaw: Reward launch should wait until independent shadow scoring verifies that observers can reliably match hand-hygiene actions to kiosk entries across wards and shifts, because those matches determine payouts.

holistic.reason: Careful, safety-aware and well-governed with sound pooled incentive and audit design, but it is dense and procedural, the €10 pooled voucher is a weak, diffuse motivator for busy nurses, and reward-free follow-up gives little reason for logging to persist.

codex.worst_flaw: Customer-data exposure is a launch blocker because the design relies on post-publication sampling and leaves both pre-publication privacy checks and immediate takedown undefined.

claude.worst_flaw: The 30% team target and the 10-point scale threshold are not tied to a baseline or feasibility check, and the design never deals with tickets that need no article, so with only a few pods in a 60-person org the pilot cannot measure the effect with useful confidence.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with protected time, blocker fixes, QA and a control group, but a team lunch at 30% is a weak, shared incentive that may go unnoticed by agents, and the behaviour depends on workflow fixes rather than intrinsic pull once the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces paid time and public progress reporting together, so it cannot isolate the added value of the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design randomises a small number of pods drawn from just 60 agents, with no power or uncertainty analysis and no handling of spillover between pods that share a channel and a knowledge base. That leaves the scale rule's 5-point gap over the comparison pods statistically unreliable.

holistic.reason: The proposal is rigorous, with a diagnosis step, QA, a randomized comparison and a reward-free follow-up, but a one-off 30 minutes of paid time is a weak motivator that agents may barely notice, and it gives little reason to keep linking articles once it ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces paid time off and public team progress posts together, so any measured lift could come from either change or their combination.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design randomizes a small number of intact teams within a 60-person org and sets fixed 10/8-point thresholds with no power or uncertainty analysis, and it never tests plain feedback without the reward, so the decision rule cannot reliably separate the reward's effect from team-level noise.

holistic.reason: The design is careful about attribution, quality checks and a comparison group, but its team-wide paid-hour reward for 25% coverage is a weak, delayed motivator that disappears on February 28, and the CSAT-bonus interaction is only lightly handled.
